lede: Nearly every question beginners ask about servitors can be sorted into one of four groups, and almost all of the confusion in this area comes from the questions being asked without a group attached. What is a servitor. Where did the idea come from. How many can I have. And how do I get rid of one. Each group has a fairly settled answer, and two of the four have answers that practitioners find inconvenient enough to avoid stating. This is a reference sheet rather than a sequence, and it is arranged so that you can find the answer to the question you actually arrived with.

sections.h2: What the questions have in common
p: The twenty questions that circulate about servitors are not twenty questions. They are four questions asked at different levels of abstraction, and people mix the levels when they read about the practice for the first time. Someone reads a description of a nineteenth-century ceremonial technique, meets a piece of folk advice about household spirits, and concludes that these are the same thing with different packaging.

The practical consequence of not sorting them is that answers get compared as if they were answering the same thing. The number of servitors you can hold is not comparable to the number described in folklore, because folklore was not describing your attention. Once the four groups are separated, most of the apparent contradictions in the literature resolve into different groups making claims that were never about the same subject.

sections.h2: The four groups the questions fall into
p: Group one is definitional: what is this thing, and is it a spirit, a part of myself, a symbol, or a memory. Group two is historical: where does the technique come from and what did it inherit. Group three is operational: how many, how often do they need attention, what do you feed them. Group four is custodial: how do you dismiss one, and what happens if you do not.

The reason to name the groups before answering anything is that group four is where the practice is weakest and where the questions are most honest. Beginners tend to arrive with group one questions, get a satisfying answer, and only discover group three and four when they have already built something. Answering the groups in order changes nothing about the practice and completely changes the experience of it.

sections.h2: What a servitor is, in one answer
p: The most defensible one-sentence answer available in the current literature is that a servitor is a persistent commitment, given a shape, to a repeated task. It is not a being you have acquired and it is not a piece of your soul that has detached. It is a held intention with an image attached, and the image is what makes it a servitor rather than a resolution.

The older framings treated this differently, and they are not simply wrong, they are answering a different question. Ceremonial literature describes a relationship with an attendant; the modern framing describes an attention you have allocated. Both are internally consistent. The second is easier to work with because it is falsifiable, and the first is easier to sell, which is the main reason it dominates the popular material.

The technique as most people meet it was popularised in nineteenth and twentieth century ceremonial writing and then developed by Austin Osman Spare, who framed entities as displaced parts of the self made available for work. Spare's contribution is the bit worth having, because it removes the need for an external being without requiring you to abandon the practice.

The older ceremony drew on the notion of a tutelary genius, a protective attendant spirit attached to a person or a place. That inheritance explains the vocabulary rather than the mechanics. Charge, feeding, and dismissal are terms borrowed wholesale from a tradition in which the relationship was between two parties, and carrying them over is the source of most of the confusion in this area.

sections.h2: The older idea it borrows from
p: A tutelary genius was a companion assigned to a person, understood in classical practice to be a protector rather than a servant. The assignment had a beginning, a set of duties, and an end, and the end was part of the arrangement. Everything about the modern servitor technique that feels like it needs a ritual wrapper comes from this older structure.

Knowing that the vocabulary is inherited rather than invented is genuinely useful, because it tells you which parts of the practice carry assumptions that may not apply to you. If the assignment had a term, then the question of when it ends is not an innovation you invented. It is a structural feature you dropped, and dropping it is the most common design error in modern servitor practice.

A feeding is a visualisation of a completed task. That is the whole definition and almost nobody gives it. You do not offer the servitor anything. You sit with the memory of the work already done, and that memory is the feed. The servitor's fuel is the evidence that the task happened.

This makes feedings easy and easy to skip. There is no offering to acquire, no schedule to keep, and no substance to prepare. It also makes them self-limiting in a useful way, because a servitor with no completed tasks to be fed has no fuel, and a task you never complete is a task with no servitor. If the task stops happening, the technique stops working, and that is either the design working correctly or a design that was never appropriate for the task.

sections.h2: How many you can hold, and why the number is low
p: Modern practice dropped any prohibition on a fixed number, which is true, and that freedom is the source of the most common failure in the whole area. The number is limited by attention, and the limit is real and not adjustable by will. Each active servitor is a thing you are holding in the background, and background holding is a budget you already spend on a great many things you do not think of as holding.

The reported practical ceiling is somewhere between one and three, and it varies with how demanding the tasks are. A servitor for remembering to water plants is cheap. A servitor for a task requiring judgement is not, and people who build six of the cheap kind and one of the expensive kind discover that the expensive one is the one that stops being maintained. Count what you are already holding before you build anything at all.

sections.h2: The ceiling nobody puts in a page
p: The number in the folklore is large and no serious text defends it. The number in practice is small and almost no text explains why. The reason is that the folkloric figure counts entities and the practical figure counts commitments, and a commitment is not free. You can hold a great many things you are not actively maintaining. You can actively maintain very few.

If you want a number for yourself, the only procedure that produces a real one is subtraction. Write down everything you are currently trying to remember, monitor, or keep in mind across work, home, health, and relationships. Count the items on that list. The number you get is your ceiling, and it will be lower than you expected, and it will be the correct answer rather than a conservative one.

sections.h2: The unglamorous list, written before you add one
p: This is the exercise that gets skipped, and skipping it is how people end up with four servitors and a slightly worse week than before. The list is unglamorous. Unpaid subscriptions, a promise to call somebody, a medication schedule, a deadline, a habit you are trying to hold, a person you are worried about. Most people produce between fifteen and thirty items and then look at the list differently.

A servitor is one more item on a list that is already too long, and the cost of the item is not the minutes you spend on it. It is the background presence, which is the thing you cannot switch off and which makes it slightly harder to run a life that already has too many open loops. If the list is long, the answer is to finish something on it first, not to add a magical process to a crowded desk.

sections.h2: The question with no good answer
p: Among the twenty questions, one has no defensible answer and it is asked constantly. It is whether the practice works. There is no measurement, no control, and no outcome that distinguishes a successful servitor from a person who has become better at noticing when they do a thing.

The honest response is that this is undecidable in the current state of the field, and that this is not the same as saying it is false. It means the design produces an outcome that is indistinguishable from ordinary habit formation, which is a well-documented process that works reliably and does not require a ritual. You can still use the technique. You should just not cite it as evidence for anything larger.

sections.h2: A sheet you would actually use
p: A one-page reference that survives contact with a real month has six fields. The task, in the imperative, narrow enough to observe. The trigger, the specific moment in the day when the task happens. The store, which is where the image lives and which you should choose deliberately. The sign of completion, written in a form you can tick. The date of the first feeding, which is a real task you have already done. And the dismissal date, written at creation.

The last field is the one that changes behaviour. A sheet with a dismissal date on it turns the practice into something with an end, and a practice with a written end is one you can actually evaluate at the finish. Without it, servitors accumulate, and accumulation is the failure mode that every experienced practitioner in this field recognises and that no beginner believes is going to happen to them.

sections.h2: A card, and the four sentences printed on it
p: Keep the four groups and one sentence per group. What it is: a persistent commitment given a shape. Where it came from: ceremonial literature, developed by Spare, inheriting the vocabulary of the tutelary genius. What a feeding is: a visualisation of a completed task. How many: as many as you can hold, which is fewer than you think and can only be found by subtraction.

That is a complete working reference and it fits on a card. Everything else in the literature on this subject expands one of those four answers without improving it, and the expansions are usually where the folklore gets in. If you are going to use this technique, use the version with the dismissal date, and expect the results to be indistinguishable from a habit you decided to keep.

faq: Is a servitor a real spirit, and does the answer change what I should do?

The current, better-developed framing treats a servitor as a persistent commitment given a shape, not as an acquired being. Practically, that means you treat it as a thing you maintain rather than a thing you have acquired, and you retire it deliberately. The older framing is internally consistent and is not refuted, but it carries obligations that are easier to observe under the first framing and impossible to verify under the second.
How many servitors can I safely have?

Find your ceiling by subtraction. List everything you are already trying to remember or keep in mind, count the items, and do not exceed that number. Most people arrive between one and three, and most people who build more than three are describing a phase rather than a steady state. The cost is background attention, not minutes, and background attention is the thing that gets depleted without you noticing.
What exactly do I do at a feeding?

You sit with the memory of a task you have already completed, for a couple of minutes, without adding anything. That is the practice. There is no offering, no material, and no schedule requirement. If the task has not been completed there is nothing to feed with, which is a useful diagnostic: a servitor with no completed tasks has no fuel, and the appropriate response is either to do the task or to retire the servitor.
Can I build a servitor for something other people do?

Technically the framing allows it and practically it is the worst version of the technique, because you cannot observe the trigger and you cannot complete the task, so you can never feed it. The techniques that work in that territory are not servitor practice in this sense; they are commitment devices, and the honest description of a commitment device is a note in a calendar with an emotional charge attached.
What if I just stop maintaining one?

Most likely nothing dramatic happens, which is why the field's failure mode is accumulation rather than catastrophe. The risk is not a punishment, it is a background commitment that never gets closed and never gets useful. This is the argument for writing the dismissal date at creation. A servitor you abandon silently costs you attention indefinitely, and nothing in the tradition will remind you that it is still there.
